newsitem.title: SWEDEN: NORDIC SKIING-BOTVINOV LEADS NEW BREED OF CROSS COUNTRY SKIERS.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-BOTVINOV LEADS NEW BREED OF CROSS COUNTRY SKIERS.

text.p: Russian born cross country exponent Mikhail Botvinov heads a new breed of skiers competing in the 13-race Worldloppet series.
Botvinov, who has won six of this season's Worldloppet races in Austrian colours, said the series is earning a profile as a competitive, international event.

"It's becoming tougher because a lot of international and elite skiers are taking part," Botvinov said after winning the world's longest cross country ski race, Sweden's Vasaloppet."We are all feeling more and more stress."
Botvinov, 29, a member of Russia's national team for eight years, entered the 1996-97 Worldloppet series to try to earn himself a place in the Austrian team.
Well known on the cross country circuit, he captured a 1993 world championship bronze medal for Russia.
But with finances tight in Russia, Botvinov moved to Austria eight months ago and hopes to get Austrian citizenship this summer and join the national team.
He could not compete for Austria in the World Cup or World Championships this season as he is officially still a member of the Russian Ski Federation.
"(The Worldloppet series) was the one possibility for me to compete in the winter and to get into the Austrian national team," said the quietly-spoken Botvinov after clinching the 90-km Vasaloppet.
Botvinov led from start to finish in difficult, wet conditions, clocking four hours 11 minutes 41 seconds, 23 minutes off the record set by Swede Bengt Hassis in 1986.

The 75-year old race, set up to commemorate the ski journey of a 16th century Swedish king, is attracting an increasing number of foreign entrants among its 15,000 competitors from more than 30 countries.
Botvinov was the ninth ever non-Swedish victor.

Previously the Vasaloppet, which winds through the forests from Berga near Salen to Mora in central Sweden, was dominated by Nordic skiers, seeking little more than the honour of winning the respected endurance race.

But Botvinov said the type of competitor had changed since the Worldloppet race series was set up in 1979, bringing 13 of the world's cross country ski events under one umbrella and creating a new world ranking table.
Worldloppet races are held each year in Australia, Germany, Austria, Japan, Italy, Estonia, Canada, Finland, France, the United States, Switzerland, and Norway.

"Some races like the Vasaloppet have such good prizes (with a top prize of 50,000 crowns ($6,500) and a trophy worth the same amount as well as spot prizes) that more people want to compete," Botvinov said.
"It is becoming a more and more recognised sport so there is more sponsorship money. If you are good you can just about make a living out of it."
This year four of the top 10 skiers in the Vasaloppet were from outside Sweden while 10 years ago only two were non-Swedes. Forty years ago there were no foreigners at all in the winning list.
Botvinov said winning the Vasaloppet was important to him.
"It is the largest race in the series and it always has very good competitors so it is a hard competition," he said.
"To win the Vasaloppet is like winning the Olympics of the Worldloppet series."
The Vasaloppet, held on the first Sunday of March every year, is one of Sweden's most popular sporting events.
More than two million of Sweden's 8.8 million population watch the televised race held in picturesque Dalarna country, 300 kms northwest of Stockholm.

"The event was designed to be an endurance test. In 1994 about 1,600 people did not make it to the end but that was a bad year with a lot of snow and slippery tracks," the Vasaloppet's managing director Mats Budh said.

The race, which began in 1922 with 136 competitors, commemorates the 400th anniversary of Gustav Vasa's historic ski journey to lead a revolt against Danish tyrant King Christian the Second, who was ruling Sweden at the time.
Gustav Vasa, a young, unknown Swede, was fleeing from the Danes, heading towards Norway after trying unsuccessfully to rally troops for a rebellion.
But at the last moment two men from Dalarna reached him to tell him their comrades would back his revolt.
Their journey on skis from Salen, where the men stopped Gustav Vasa, back to Mora, where the rebels went into battle against the Danish occupiers, is the path of the Vasaloppet.
The insurgency was successful and Gustav Vasa was proclaimed king of Sweden on June 6, 1523.
